paragraphs: The following assessments concern on-site work practices for locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants; they do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or contract outcomes.

Locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants safeguard and issue items according to venue rules: providing guests with personal items and supplies such as towels, clothing, and sports equipment, assigning lockers or clothing containers and issuing and collecting claim checks, collecting laundry and maintaining lost-and-found and item inventories, cleaning and organizing premises and footwear, answering questions, helping open doors or move luggage, and reporting safety issues or complaints.

Wholly fictional service-desk sample: given a fictional locker room or coatroom duty scenario containing 1 item and locker allocation list, 1 claim-check mismatch, 1 customer complaint, and 1 safety hazard, write item issue and return records, claim-check verification, complaint and hazard reports, and shift handover records within 45 minutes. Do not use real customer information or employer secrets.

Sample outputs and reflection: check whether claim checks and items are verified under rules, lost-and-found and handover records are retained, and complaints and safety hazards are reported. Then consider whether you can remain patient during prolonged standing and repetitive service, strictly follow venue rules and keep accurate records, and accept responsibility for safeguarding belongings.

Locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants on this page means O*NET 39-3093.00: providing personal items and supplies such as towels, clothing, and sports equipment in changing rooms, coatrooms, or storage rooms; assigning lockers or clothing containers and issuing claim checks; collecting laundry, maintaining lost-and-found and item inventories, cleaning premises, answering questions, and assisting customers. Work is mainly in indoor service venues such as fitness, recreation, accommodation, and food service settings, emphasizing rule execution, safeguarding belongings, and service. This page excludes related roles such as baggage porters and bellhops, hotel desk clerks, and food servers.

entries: Work inputs: guests' personal items and supplies such as towels, clothing, footwear, and sports equipment; lockers and clothing containers; claim checks and lost-and-found; laundry and cleaning supplies; premises and equipment; venue rules and safety requirements.

Verifiable outputs: accurate item issue and return records, locker and storage assignments matching claim checks, maintained lost-and-found and item inventories, cleaned premises and equipment, and complaint and hazard reports.

Complete workflow: check items and premises at shift start → issue supplies and assign lockers or storage spaces → verify and collect claim checks → collect laundry and replenish supplies → clean and organize premises and maintain lost-and-found → handle questions and complaints and report safety hazards → hand over and record.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether items match claim checks, lockers or storage spaces are assigned under rules, which items need laundry or repair, when complaints and safety hazards must be reported, and which actions exceed job authority.

O*NET work context survey: 81% of respondents reported standing continually or almost continually, and 64% reported a typical workweek under 40 hours. Handling items and communicating with guests are frequent. Verify shifts, weekend peaks, and venue conditions at the target site; survey proportions do not establish every role's arrangements.

Research inputs: O*NET 39-3093.00 occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, interest code, and tools and technology. Use findings within the exact U.S. occupational scope; do not infer mainland China qualification, wage, or employment definitions.

Check first: quantities and condition of shift items and lockers, handover matters and lost-item lists, venue rules and safety requirements, items needing laundry or repair, and hazards and complaints requiring reports.

Complete workflow: shift-start checks, item issue and locker assignments, claim-check verification and collection, cleaning and replenishment, complaint and hazard reporting, and shift handover records. Do not proceed before items and claim checks are verified.

Related responsibility boundaries: this page covers locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants only. Baggage porters and bellhops handle luggage, hotel desk clerks handle registration and accounts, and food servers handle orders and meal service. Authority and final responsibilities are not interchangeable with this page.

Waiters and waitresses take orders, serve food, and settle bills as direct participants in food service. Locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants focus on safeguarding and issuing items and maintaining premises rather than food service and billing.

Nonrestaurant food servers provide food and nonalcoholic beverages at banquets, institutions, and similar settings. Locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants handle clothing, towels, and storage, with different work objects.

Hotel, motel, and resort desk clerks handle registration, reservations, accounts, and customer issue escalation. Locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants safeguard items and maintain premises rather than handle accounts or room bookings.

Counter and rental clerks arrange rentals, take payments, and check returns of merchandise or equipment. Locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants safeguard guests' personal items and lockers, usually without cashiering or merchandise sales.
AI Impact Boundaries for Locker Room, Coatroom, and Dressing Room Attendants

Editorial tool-trial candidates: use fictional item lists to test registration, inventory reminders, and handover record organization. The existence of registration, scheduling, or monitoring systems does not establish AI capabilities or actual adoption. Responsible personnel confirm items, claim checks, customer communication, and hazard reports under venue rules.

Occupational sources describe actual tasks and work objects—item issue and return, lockers and claim checks, laundry and cleaning, lost-and-found, and premises maintenance. Record tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes separately; wage or employment data do not replace AI evidence.

Registration, inventory reminders, and record organization are candidates awaiting validation. This round established neither task automation difficulty nor impact sequencing. Human responsibility remains for on-site item checks, lost-item confirmation, and customer conflict handling.

Human control points include checking items and claim checks, confirming locker assignments, deciding when to report complaints or hazards, and taking responsibility for safeguarding belongings and records.
First use wholly fictional allocation lists and duty scenarios for an offline checking exercise. Record judgments and reporting paths; do not let unverified automation prompts replace on-site checks.
Editorial suggestion: tools may assist item registration, inventory reminders, and cleaning schedules. Current materials do not establish widespread adoption of these systems in this occupation.
Verify against on-site items and claim checks, and retain human confirmations and reports.

Mainland China wage boundary: National Bureau of Statistics industry materials reviewed this round established no separate correspondence for this occupation. Culture, sports, and entertainment provides a broad industry reference for recreation venues, not proof that most workers in this occupation belong to that industry. Verify the actual employer industry.

All are industry-scope figures, not this occupation's median or starting pay.

This page has not obtained an entry precisely matching O*NET 39-3093.00 and does not treat it as a national occupational median. Refer to the competent authority's publications.

This page displays labeled industry proxies only and does not fill the gap with proxy or U.S. figures.
U.S. Locker Room, Coatroom, and Dressing Room Attendant Pay and Employment Scope

U.S. national 2025 OEWS median annual pay is 36,300 USD and median hourly pay is 17.45 USD, with the 10th—90th percentiles ranging from 26,590—54,260 USD. Separate figures show 16,000 employed in 2025 and a projected 17,100 in 2035, 6% growth for 2025—2035, and 4,000 average annual openings from growth and replacement.

National wage percentiles are not starting pay or individual take-home income. O*NET's hours distribution does not establish payment methods. This round obtained no evidence of the prevalence of tips or hourly pay in this occupation; verify payment arrangements in each job contract.
The 10th and 90th percentiles describe national wage distribution boundaries, not experience levels. The table cannot estimate the effects of hours, venue type, or tips.

O*NET2025 industry employment shares: arts, entertainment, and recreation 37%; accommodation and food services 22%; other services except public administration 21%. These describe employer settings, not wages or future demand projections.

2025 employment is 16,000, with projected growth of 6% for 2025—2035. The 4,000 average annual openings include replacements, not 4,000 net new jobs each year or current recruitment counts; do not extrapolate individual opportunities across regions.
Fit Signals: Start with Observable Work Behaviors

To assess fit, first consider whether you can maintain consistency during prolonged standing and repetitive service, strictly follow item and claim-check rules, patiently handle customer questions and complaints, and accept responsibility for safeguarding belongings and reporting safety issues. RIASEC and similar tools can only suggest hypotheses; they cannot replace actual task experience.

Positive signals: reliability and attention to detail, rule-based item and claim-check verification, willingness to clean and organize proactively, and patience and accurate records when many customers are present.

Conditions requiring caution: unwillingness to stand and walk for extended periods, impatience with repetitive service, discomfort with brief but frequent guest communication, or difficulty strictly following property safeguarding rules.

Trial action: use wholly fictional allocation lists and duty scenarios to practice item issue and return, claim-check verification, and complaint or hazard reporting, then write shift handover records. Ask someone else to verify using the records.

The RIASEC interest code is CRS (Conventional—Realistic—Social), emphasizing procedural tasks, hands-on cleaning and organization, and service to others. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence, qualifications, or authorization.

Insufficient evidence: this round obtained no personality predictive validity research for this occupation. Observe behavior using fictional item-checking, lost-item registration, and customer communication samples; personality measures support reflection only.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications; use them for self-reflection only.

Entry Paths and Capability Stages

O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone1—2. The few days to one year of training is a group description, not a fixed training duration for this occupation. In the education survey, 64% of respondents said new hires need high school or equivalent, while 20% selected less than high school. These are judgments of education needs, not workers' attainment distribution. Verify specific entry training by venue.

For the United States and mainland China separately, verify the target venue's training and authorization for property custody, key management, cashiering, and emergencies. Insufficient evidence: this round did not establish a complete correspondence with specific entry requirements in either place; O*NET codes do not imply that qualifications are unnecessary.

Job training records and work authorization are different statuses. Completing training does not automatically grant key management, cashiering, or emergency command authority. Refer matters beyond role and authorization scope to responsible personnel.
Entry stage: under supervision, practice item issue and return, locker assignments, claim-check verification, and premises cleaning, retaining handover records.
Evidence to show: use verifiable item allocation and return records, lost-and-found lists, and shift handover records to demonstrate rule execution and accuracy.
Next step: check the target venue's rules, shifts, and required training, then verify item checking, customer communication, and hazard-reporting skills during supervised real shifts.

Editorial pathway example: use item and handover records to apply for inventory collaboration or training duties. Front desk, customer service, and operations are independent target roles requiring registration, systems, complaint-handling, or management evidence and employer appointment, not a mandatory promotion sequence.
Market Signals and Transition Directions

U.S. O*NET/BLS: 16,000 employed in 2025, projected to reach 17,100 in 2035, 6% growth for 2025—2035, and 4,000 average annual openings from growth and replacement. Occupational projections are not current recruitment samples or individual hiring probabilities.

2025 occupational employment shares by industry: arts, entertainment, and recreation 37%; accommodation and food services 22%; other services except public administration 21%. Shares do not represent regional recruitment demand.

Transferable skills: item registration and verification, customer communication and service, premises cleaning and organization, lost-item and inventory management, rule execution, and safety reporting.

Transition to waiter or waitress work requires order taking, meal delivery, food hygiene, cashiering, and target-venue service processes. Item verification and customer communication may transfer but do not establish food-service competence.

description.text: This page covers O*NET 39-3093.00 Locker Room, Coatroom, and Dressing Room Attendants: issuing towels, clothing, and sports equipment, assigning lockers and checking claim checks, maintaining lost-and-found and item inventories, cleaning premises, and answering customer questions. Work is mainly in indoor service venues and often involves prolonged standing. When evaluating this career, examine the complete workflow, responsibility boundaries, evidence definitions, risk controls, and observable entry-level work samples together.

subject.name: Locker Room, Coatroom, and Dressing Room Attendants
subject.summary: This page covers O*NET 39-3093.00 Locker Room, Coatroom, and Dressing Room Attendants: issuing personal items such as towels, clothing, and sports equipment to guests in changing rooms, coatrooms, or storage rooms; assigning lockers or clothing containers and issuing, checking, and collecting claim checks; collecting laundry, maintaining lost-and-found and item inventories, cleaning and organizing premises and footwear; answering questions, helping open doors or move luggage, and reporting safety issues or complaints. Work is mainly in indoor service venues such as fitness, recreation, accommodation, and food service settings, emphasizing rule execution, safeguarding belongings, and customer service. This page excludes related roles such as baggage porters and bellhops, hotel desk clerks, and food servers.
